newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIA NAPHTHA/MOGAS -SOFTER WITH CRUDE, WEAK DEMAND.
newsitem.headline: ASIA NAPHTHA/MOGAS -SOFTER WITH CRUDE, WEAK DEMAND.

text.p: Light distillates fell on Friday on the back of softer crude and weak demand, traders said.
Iraq was expected to start exporting crude oil by as early as next week, dragging Brent crude prices down in past two consecutive days.
September Brent on SIMEX last traded $18.86 per barrel, down four cents, after London fell 30 cents overnight.
Gasoline prices in the U.S. also fell sharply amid talk of more imports arriving to ease the supply tightness.
Singapore fob sellers emerged at lower levels with the 95-octane offered at $22.90 per barrel compared to Thursday's $23.10.
Unleaded 97-octane unleaded was sold by a U.S. major at $24.90 fob Singapore lifting August 23-27, to a European major.
Traders were still bearish on the gasoline outlook despite the Philippines taking out some August and September supplies, but it was "no great shakes".
Demand was mainly for the high-octane which was still tight amid high prices of blending component MTBE and cuts in reforming output.
But refiners were maintaining their reforming output to around 70-80-percent.
"The margin is still not there," said one refiner.
But the market was looking ahead to Taiwan's reformate import tender which closes on Monday for further direction.
Taiwan is expected to buy two 250,00-barrel cargoes for September after it cancelled its tender for the first half due to high offers.
Naphtha also fell with August losing 40-45 cents per barrel to $21.35/$21.45.
September was last quoted in a slight contango at $21.30/$21.55 as the prompt market was under pressure from supplies and weak regional demand.
Half month spreads in October open-spec levels were in a contango of $1.00-$1.50 per tonne.
Endusers in North Asia were reporting high stocks as demand has dropped amid poor petrochemical -- polyethylene and polypropylene -- prices.

The weak petrochemical market is expected to weigh down on the naphtha market and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co's (ADNOC) chances of getting consensus from term buyers on its offer for about 200,000 tonnes lifting between September 1997-July 1998.
ADNOC offer stands at $22 per tonne over its formula, on a free-on-board basis, compared to current term prices of $7.15.
Traders said buyers -- a Japanese oil firm and a Japanese trading arm of a European major -- are likely to aim for prices lower than the latest ADNOC premium of $21 for July 1997-June 1998 supplies.
(Prices are in dollars per barrel)
